title: The Xylos Moon Mystery
markdown:
Brilliant twin suns splashed gold and lavender across the sky above Xylos Moon. Dawn broke. Colors exploded. Vik, the apprentice geologist, practically bounced out of his cot. Boots thumped a quick rhythm on the cool metal floor. The Harvest Festival. A new colony on a vibrant world. Pure sparkling possibility. He grabbed his trusty rock hammer, polished head gleaming like a tiny sun.

“Time to dig.”

Down the corridor, Nara, the mayor’s son, was already straightening his crisply pressed uniform.

“Careful, Vik. This moon is still new. We need to respect it, truly understand it, before we poke around and make a mess.”

Vik grinned. The thrill of discovery buzzed like a sparkler. He loved how Nara always thought things through. Mayor Thorne, Nara’s father, believed in progress above all else. But today was for celebrating.

Drillbit, their sturdy terrain probe, whirred to life near the main plaza. Treads click-clacked. Gleaming metallic body ready. It scanned, recorded, guarded them from unstable moon-rock.

“Festival protocols initiated. All clear for celebratory seismic activity, provided it remains within standard parameters.”

Then it happened.

A deep jarring shake. Not the soft familiar thrum of moon-quakes. A sharp percussive jolt sent colorful festival decorations tumbling. A collective gasp. The upbeat music faltered, then died. Shocked silence.

Vik’s eyes widened. “Whoa. That wasn’t a typical tremor.” His hand tightened on the hammer. “That felt purposeful.”

Nara’s brow furrowed. Gaze on the scanner at his wrist. “Seismic readings are spiking. But the frequency is odd. Too regular. Almost like a heartbeat.”

Drillbit’s optical sensors swiveled, a rapid clicking. “Anomaly detected. Unusual subterranean vibration pattern. Probability of standard geological event: 3.7 percent.”

“Three point seven?” Vik’s voice jumped. “That means it’s not standard. This is our chance, Nara. To find out what’s making it shake.” Infinitely more thrilling than any festival.

Nara hesitated. He glanced toward his father, already stepping forward to calm the crowd. The determined glint in Vik’s eyes was infectious.

“All right. But we’re careful. And we’re quick. We stick together.”

“Buckle up. Because this part is going to be interesting.”

With a shared nod the three dashed from the stunned festival-goers, boots kicking up dust, following the rhythmic pulse of the moon.

Across the crater the ground cracked open. Not violently. A strange deliberate grind. They scrambled to avoid falling rocks as a section of floor fell away with a dull thud. Below, not more rock, but a dull metallic sheen glinted in the twin suns.

“What is that?” Nara whispered, peering into the dark crevice. A cold prickle down his spine. Unlike any sight Xylos had revealed.

Vik scrambled down. Geologist’s instinct pushing aside hesitation. He scraped loose dust with his hammer. More of the strange material.

“It’s machinery. Ancient. Look.” Intricate copper-like conduits and interlocking gears. Silent. Still. Buried deep. The bones of a sleeping giant.

Drillbit’s scanners whirred into overdrive. “Subterranean network detected. Massive. Estimated age: millennia. Power signature: dormant, but resonant. Unlike anything in our databanks.”

“Dormant?” Vik looked back toward the festival. Another rumble, louder, shaking the air. “But those tremors are getting stronger. Like something is trying to wake up.”

Nara’s face paled. Caution returned. “The mining. Our new deep-core drills. They’re probably hitting something these machines don’t like.” He remembered his father’s speeches about unlocking mineral wealth, digging deeper than ever. Progress suddenly felt like a dangerous force.

“They’re not just machines,” Drillbit said, losing its usual calm. “Deep scans indicate an ancient terraforming system. Vastly complex. Powerful. And it’s waking up. The tremors are not just a warning. They’re a reaction.”

They had to tell someone. They raced toward the colony hub.

Mayor Thorne and the council were too busy managing the festival’s disruption.

“Geological anomalies, Vik? Nonsense.” A dismissive hand. “We have a celebration to finish. Get back to your studies. We can’t afford every little geological quirk.”

“But Father, it’s not just rocks.” Nara stepped forward, desperate. “The machines are ancient. Our mining is disturbing them. It’s dangerous.”

“Nonsense.” Face set like stone. “This colony needs resources. We can’t stop for every little shake.”

The ground bucked violently. The festival stage tilted. Screams. Drillbit’s alarm blared.

“Seismic activity escalating exponentially. Imminent structural collapse. Terraforming systems activating fully. This is not a drill.”

A huge section of the main dome groaned, a terrible tearing. Dust rained like gritty snow. A miner barely scrambled clear as a tunnel entrance caved with a deafening roar. Sharp metallic scent. The point of no return.

Vik’s heart hammered. Cold dread. His knowledge, his tools, not enough against machines so vast. He looked at Nara, face etched with worry, not just for their home but for a father who still refused to see.

“We’re too late,” Nara whispered. Energy drained.

Vik’s gaze swept the panicked faces, the crumbling structures. On his scanner feed the deep-core drill thudded, echoing the machine’s pulse. A spark.

“No. We’re not. The drills. Their frequency. It’s what’s waking them, but it’s also the key.”

“The key?” Hope flickered.

“If we broadcast a counter-frequency, a stabilizing signal, we can calm them. Stop the collapse.”

“How?”

“The main mining hub. Modify the drill’s transmitter. Drillbit, can you get us there fast?”

“Affirmative.” Rotors spun. A determined hum.

They bolted. Ground trembling. A deep mechanical groan from the moon’s core. At the hub Vik nearly slipped on spilled coolant, then found the transmitter housing already warm from the drill’s own hunger. He worked feverishly, hands flying over the panel, wires sparking. Nara stood guard at the door, heart pounding, and once shoved a crate against a buckling strut so Vik would not have to look up. Drillbit projected schematics, metallic voice steady, then dimmed its optics so Vik could see the last solder without glare.

“Almost there. One more connection.” Vik slammed a large red button.

A high-pitched whine fought the ominous rumble. Tremors lessened. Groaning subsided into a soft steady hum. The machines, poised to fully awaken, seemed to pause. A deep calming breath.

Nara burst through the council doors, Vik and Drillbit close behind.

“Stop the drills. Now.” An authority he had never known. His father bewildered among confused council members. “We’ve discovered an ancient network. A terraforming system. Our mining is destroying it, and ourselves. Vik figured out how to stabilize it. But we have to change our plan. Work with it, not against it.”

Mayor Thorne stared at the console. Frantic spikes replaced by calm rhythmic lines. He saw the truth in his son’s face.

“Change our plan,” he murmured. A different kind of progress dawned.

The festival resumed, quieter, filled with a hushed respect. Someone righted a fallen garland and did not put the music back on at once. Colonists spoke of the ancient network they would now protect. A child asked Vik if the moon had a heart; he showed her the scanner instead of answering. Vik, Nara, and Drillbit stood at the edge of the colony and watched the twin suns begin their descent, orange and purple, Drillbit’s treads still ticking as if counting a safer rhythm.

Vik did not declare what they would build next. Nara only looked out at the vast unknown landscape, then at the quiet scanner on his wrist, the heartbeat now a sleeping one, and did not put the uniform’s last crease back into place.
